result:
Have you ever stared at an antique map and noticed how the cartographers filled the empty spaces? Where knowledge ended, imagination took over. Sea serpents coiled in uncharted oceans, and winged lions guarded the edges of unknown continents. "Here be dragons" was rarely written literally, yet the sentiment lingered in every swirling ink line. Those blank margins were invitations, promising that the world was still vast enough to hide wonders.

Today, our maps fit inside glowing glass rectangles. We can zoom in until we see the cracked pavement outside a bakery three thousand miles away. Satellite eyes leave no corner unlit, no valley unmeasured. On the surface, it seems the mystery has been scrubbed clean from the earth, replaced by blue dots and estimated arrival times. We rarely get lost anymore, which means we rarely stumble upon things we were not looking for.

Yet, the uncharted territories have not vanished; they have simply migrated inward. The deepest oceans now reside in human memory, in faded dreams, and in the quiet spaces between words during an honest conversation. Every stranger passing on a rainy street carries an entire continent of untold stories, complete with forgotten ruins, hidden rivers, and sudden, breathtaking vistas.

Perhaps we never needed sea monsters to make the world feel magical. We only needed the humility to admit how little we truly understand, and the stubborn curiosity to keep wandering past the familiar boundaries of everything we already know, trusting that discovery still waits just beyond our sight.
